subtype: Approach: adjust routines to reduce stress while waiting [Revision]
passage:
Jasleen's scan results were due in ten days, and for the first four she barely slept. Every night in her Chandigarh flat she lay with her phone above her face, reading about what the scan might show, until two or three in the morning. By day she snapped at her brother Kishore and forgot her lunch.
On the fifth morning she noticed it: the fear was always worst after the scrolling, and lighter by afternoon. So she changed the rules. Phone on the kitchen shelf at 11 p.m., lights off at 11:30. A walk around the garden near her building every evening, with Kishore coming along when he could. And if she needed to look something up, one fifteen-minute slot after lunch, then the tab closed.
The first night she lay awake anyway. By the third, she slept till seven. The results were still days away. But she was meeting them with some energy left.

qa.q: When does Jasleen put her phone on the kitchen shelf?
qa.a: At 11 p.m.

qa.q: How did the late-night scrolling affect how Jasleen felt?
qa.a: It made her more frightened and sleepless, so by day she was short-tempered and forgetful.

qa.q: What else could help Jasleen until the results come?
qa.a: Asking the clinic whom to call with questions, and planning something small each day with Kishore to fill the wait.

qa.q: What is the wait like for Kishore?
qa.a: Kishore is snapped at early on, then becomes part of the fix, walking with her in the evenings.

grounding: Shows a young person noticing that night scrolling raises fear while waiting for results, and setting a sleep time, daily walks and one short search slot.

'You're up again?' Uma switched on the kitchen light. It was 2 a.m. 'Sonali. Phone down.'
'Maa, I'm just reading what the results could mean.'
'Since when?'
Sonali looked at the screen. 'Since eleven.'
'And do you feel better or worse?'
A long pause. 'Worse. Every night, worse.'
'Then that's your answer.' Uma sat down across from her. 'The report comes on Friday. What would help you get to Friday?'
'Sleeping, I guess. Not reading this at night.'
'So?'
'So the phone stays in your room after ten-thirty.' Sonali half laughed. 'And I'll walk with you in the mornings, like before exams.'
'And the reading?'
'Once a day. Fifteen minutes. After lunch.'
'Write it on the fridge.'
On Thursday night Sonali handed her phone over at ten-thirty without being asked. 'Still scared,' she said. 'But less tired.'

qa.q: When does the report come?
qa.a: On Friday.

qa.q: How does Sonali feel on Thursday night?
qa.a: Still scared about the report, but less tired and steadier than before.

qa.a: Uma sees it making her daughter worse and asks questions until Sonali decides the new rules herself.

subtype: Approach: follow the treatment plan with a reminder routine [Action]

Monday, 8 p.m. Kiran's diary.
It's official now. The doctor said it's a long-term thing and manageable if I follow the plan properly. I came home and cried for a while, then made tea and got organised, because crying wasn't going to remember anything for me.
What I did tonight:
1. Wrote the doctor's instructions in the front of this diary, word for word from the prescription sheet, including the foods to go easy on.
2. Set phone reminders for the medicines, the blood test on the 14th, and the follow-up on the 28th.
3. Put every report so far into a blue folder, dated, oldest at the back.
Tarun saw the folder and said, 'You've become an office.' He's also set a reminder on his own phone for the 14th so he can come with me.
It's a lot. But it's written down, so it's not all in my head.

qa.a: On the 14th.

subtype: Approach: rely on a home remedy from a relative instead of a check-up [Pitfall]

Swati's ear had been aching for a week when Simran Masi came to stay at their flat in Lucknow. 'Warm mustard oil with garlic at night,' Masi said, patting her cheek. 'It's nothing, beta. We never went to doctors for such small things.'
It felt good to hear. Masi's voice was so sure, and the clinic meant taking leave from her new office job. So every night Masi warmed the oil, and Swati said the ache felt a little better, because she wanted it to.
By the third week she could barely hear on that side, and chewing brought a sharp pain. On Monday she finally went to an ENT clinic. The doctor examined her ear, asked about the oil, and said she should have come sooner; treatment would now take longer.
At home Masi was quiet. 'I thought I was helping,' she said.
'You were being kind,' Swati said. 'I just needed kind and a doctor.'

qa.q: What remedy did Simran Masi suggest?
qa.a: Warm mustard oil with garlic at night.

qa.q: Why did Swati go along with the oil for so long?
qa.a: Masi's certainty felt comforting and Swati wanted it to be nothing, so she felt reassured instead of checking.

qa.q: What could Swati have done while still respecting Masi?
qa.a: Thanked Masi and booked a clinic visit anyway once the ache kept going; kindness and a check-up can go together.

qa.q: How does Simran Masi feel when the truth comes out?
qa.a: Quiet and regretful, having meant only to help, and perhaps hurt that her reassurance delayed care.

grounding: Shows a young person trusting a relative's comforting home remedy and reassurance, delaying a check-up until the problem is worse.

'Still that cough?' Nani asked, stirring the pot. 'I'll make you kadha. Tulsi, ginger, honey. It's the weather, jaanu, nothing else.'
'You think so, Nani?'
'I know so. Your mother had the same every winter.'
Dilnaz drank the kadha that night, and the next, and the next. It was warm and tasted like being small. Nani's certainty felt like a blanket.
Three weeks later, at the office, her colleague Francis looked up from his desk. 'Dilnaz, you've been coughing since before Diwali.'
'My Nani's treating it.'
'With what?'
'Kadha.'
'Has a doctor heard it?'
She stopped. 'No.'
'Why not?'
'Because Nani said it was nothing.' She heard how it sounded. 'And because I wanted it to be nothing.'
'The clinic downstairs is open till six.'
She went at five. The doctor listened to her chest for a long time and ordered an X-ray. On the way home she wondered how to tell Nani.

qa.a: Tulsi, ginger, honey.

qa.a: Dilnaz was comforted by Nani's certainty and afraid of a worse answer, so she let comfort stand in for checking.

subtype: Approach: notice the pattern through a mood diary [Thinking]
passage:
Counsellor's note, 22 January. Yogesh, student wellbeing centre.
Anjali, final-year B.Sc., came for her second session and brought a small notebook. At our first meeting she had described feeling 'flat, not sad exactly, just grey' for about five weeks, and I had asked if she might note a few things each day. She did more than that.
Every evening she had written three lines: hours slept, whether she ate properly, and a mood score out of ten. On her own, she had added a line for 'saw people today, yes or no'.
She had spotted the pattern before I said anything. 'The low days come after nights I stay up past three, and days I don't leave my room,' she said. 'I thought it was random. It isn't.'
She seemed relieved to have something concrete. We agreed on two small experiments for the next fortnight, and she will keep the diary going. Next session: 5 February.

qa.q: What line did Anjali add on her own?
qa.a: 'Saw people today, yes or no'.

qa.q: How did Anjali seem to feel on spotting the pattern?
qa.a: Relieved to have something concrete, after weeks of feeling flat and grey without knowing why.

qa.q: What experiments might follow from Anjali's own pattern?
qa.a: Keeping a regular bedtime and planning to see someone each day, then checking whether the low days change.

qa.q: How does the session look to Yogesh, the counsellor who wrote the note?
qa.a: Yogesh sees Anjali find the pattern herself, and builds the next steps on that rather than supplying the answer.

grounding: Shows a final-year student tracking sleep, food and mood, seeing a link with late nights and isolation, and bringing it to a counsellor.

Sunday, 9 March. Nazia's diary.
Three weeks of this notebook now. The college counsellor, Arohi ma'am, asked me to try it: sleep, food, mood out of ten, anything else I notice. I thought it would be pointless.
Tonight I spread the pages on my bed and looked at them all at once.
Mood 3 or 4: the day after I slept at 3 a.m. or later. Every time.
Mood 3: days I ate only instant noodles in my room and saw nobody.
Mood 6: the two Saturdays I studied in the library with my lab partner, and the day Ammi visited.
So it isn't me being lazy or broken. There's a pattern. Late nights plus being alone equals grey.
I'm taking the notebook to Arohi ma'am on Tuesday. I underlined the pattern in red so I don't lose my nerve and say 'I'm fine' like I usually do.
Small thing, but I'm going to bed at midnight tonight. Let's see what Monday says.

qa.a: On Tuesday.

qa.a: Nazia had been self-blaming and now feels relieved and a little hopeful, seeing that the low mood follows a pattern.

qa.q: What could Nazia try this week, based on the notebook?
qa.a: Earlier nights and planned time with people, like the library Saturdays, then checking whether the mood scores change.

I'm Mridul, Yogesh's closest friend since first year. For most of October he'd been quieter than usual: skipping cricket, eating late, saying 'just tired' when I asked.
One night on the hostel terrace he said it without me asking. 'Everything's been heavy for about a month. Not one reason. Just heavy.' He said it fast, looking at the water tank, as if he'd practised it.
I didn't have answers. I said, 'Thanks for telling me. What would help?' He said he didn't know yet, but it already felt a bit lighter just having said it.
The next evening he called his sister Prerna in Nagpur, with me sitting nearby 'for courage', he said. She listened for a long time, then helped him book a slot at the college counselling centre for that Friday, and said she would call him every Sunday.
I can't know how heavy it still is. But he came to cricket on Saturday.

qa.q: How long had things felt heavy for Yogesh?
qa.a: About a month.

qa.a: A little lighter, relieved to have said it aloud even without answers yet.

Monday. Damini hasn't told anyone. For a month her days have felt like wading through water. She goes to lectures, smiles, comes back and lies on her bed until it's dark. When her friend Ruchika asks her to the canteen, she says she has a headache.
Wednesday. In the library stairwell, Ruchika asks again, gently. This time Damini says, 'I'm not okay. It's been heavy for about a month.' Her voice cracks on 'month'. Ruchika sits on the step beside her. 'Thank you for telling me. Would you call your sister? I'll stay.' That evening, with Ruchika beside her, Damini calls her older sister Lavanya in Bengaluru. Lavanya listens without interrupting, then says, 'I'm glad you called. Let's find the counselling centre's number together, right now.' They book a Friday slot before the call ends.
Friday. Ruchika waits outside the counselling room. Afterwards Damini eats dinner in the canteen for the first time in weeks.

I'm Kunal. In March I went to the campus doctor, Dr Vijay, about headaches and not sleeping. After a few questions, the doctor asked how my mood had been, and I surprised myself by telling the truth: low for about two months, nothing feels worth doing, stopped going to practice. Dr Vijay said it was worth talking to someone trained for this, and gave me the college counselling centre's number and a helpline in case things felt worse before the appointment.
I walked around campus for twenty minutes before calling. Part of me thought counselling was for people with 'real' problems. Then I thought: I came to a doctor for headaches without feeling weak. This is the same.
I booked Thursday at 4. That night I wrote half a page to take with me: sleeping badly for two months, not hungry, stopped football, feeling far away from friends, worse on Sundays.
On Thursday my hands were cold. But I had the page, and I read from it.

qa.a: Thursday at 4.

qa.a: It lets Kunal share the main points even with cold hands and nerves, so nothing important is left unsaid.

qa.a: As an important step, since asking about mood uncovered more than headaches and led to the right kind of help.

Warden's note, Block B, 14 November. Shalini.
Deepika, second year, came to my office this evening and asked, very quietly, how students book the college counsellor. She said she had been 'not herself' for weeks: sleeping in the afternoons, skipping the mess, crying after calls home without knowing why. She added quickly, 'It's probably nothing. Before she left, she asked for paper and wrote a few lines to take to the session: when it started, what has changed, what she hopes for. She folded it into her ID card holder.

subtype: Approach: push through and hide it [Pitfall]
passage:
It was the last month of Zubin's internship at an architecture firm in Ahmedabad, with the final presentation on the 30th and everyone watching to see who would get an offer. So when the heaviness came back, he decided nobody would see it.
At the office he was the funny one, making chai for the team, laughing in every meeting. At the flat he skipped dinner most nights and lay in the dark with his phone face down. Madhav's messages piled up unread: 'cricket Sunday?', 'you alive?', 'hello??'
He told himself that admitting it would look weak, right when he needed to look strong. But the smiling took everything. By the third week he was making mistakes in drawings he could once do half asleep.
Two days before the presentation, Madhav turned up with food. Zubin opened the door with his office smile. Madhav looked at the empty fridge and said quietly, 'You don't have to do that face with me.'
Zubin sat down on the floor. Then, for the first time in a month, he told someone.

qa.q: When was the final presentation?
qa.a: On the 30th.

qa.q: Why did Zubin hide how he felt?
qa.a: He felt ashamed of struggling and pressured to look strong for the offer, so admitting it seemed weak and he kept smiling.

qa.q: What could Zubin have done in the first week instead?
qa.a: Told Madhav or a counsellor that the heaviness was back, so support came before his energy ran out.

qa.q: What was it like for Madhav as the messages went unanswered?
qa.a: Madhav grew worried enough to turn up with food, and gently let Zubin drop the act.

grounding: Shows a young person keeping a cheerful face at work while skipping meals and ignoring friends, which drains energy and delays help.

After the placement results came out and his name wasn't on any list, Chaitanya decided he would be fine in public. In the hostel group chat he sent jokes. In the corridor of his Hyderabad college he high-fived everyone who had an offer.
In his room he wasn't fine. He stopped going to the mess and lived on biscuits. He stopped answering his school friends, because typing 'all good' again felt like lifting something heavy. He slept till noon and then felt worse.
His roommate, Zubin, noticed only because the biscuit wrappers kept piling up. 'You're the happiest person in the group chat,' Zubin said one night, 'and I haven't seen you eat a meal in a week.'
Chaitanya laughed. Then he stopped laughing. 'I didn't want anyone to think I can't handle it.'
Zubin sat on the other bed. 'I'd rather you couldn't handle it with me than alone. Call your brother tonight? And we'll see the placement mentor tomorrow.'
Chaitanya picked up his phone and called his brother.

qa.a: He lived on biscuits.

subtype: Approach: cut all plans down to a minimum routine [Thinking]

Reena, you say even getting out of bed feels like climbing a hill some days. I believe you. Let your Bhupen mama tell you about a winter when I was twenty and felt the same.
I'd moved to Shillong for my first job, and somewhere in that cold, grey season everything went heavy. Every night I made lists: exercise, study for the bank exam, write home, clean the room. Each morning I did none of it, and felt worse for failing.
One Sunday I tore up the long list and asked myself: what is the smallest day I can still call a day? I wrote three things only. Get up at seven. Eat one proper meal, not tea and biscuits. Go outside for ten minutes, even just to the corner shop.
Some days that was all I did. But I did it, and it held me steady till spring. That spring I also went to a doctor, which I should have done sooner.
So, Reena. Three things. That's allowed.

qa.q: What were the three things on young Bhupen's short list?
qa.a: Get up at seven, eat one proper meal, go outside for ten minutes.

qa.q: How did young Bhupen feel after failing the long lists each morning?
qa.a: Worse and more discouraged, as each unfinished list felt like another failure.

qa.q: What was the turning point in Bhupen's story, and why did it help?
qa.a: Tearing up the long list for three small tasks; they were possible even on heavy days, so each day ended with something done.

qa.q: What would change if young Bhupen had kept the long lists?
qa.a: Each morning would likely have added another failure, deepening the heaviness instead of holding things steady.

grounding: Shows a person on low days cutting plans to three tasks: waking at a set time, eating properly and stepping outside briefly.

passage:
Semester exams started in nine days, the hostel internet had been down since Monday, and Sumit had spent three mornings in bed until noon, staring at a timetable that said 'revise four chapters a day'.
On Thursday his friend Hafsa, a senior who had once had a rough semester of her own, called from the next block. He admitted it: 'I can't do any of it. I just lie there.'
'Then don't do any of it,' she said. 'What's the least you can do and still call it a day?'
He thought aloud, slowly. 'Wake at eight. Eat breakfast in the mess, not just chai. Walk to the library and back, even if I don't open a book.' He paused. 'Three things.'
'Three things. Text me when each one's done.'
On Friday he did all three. At the library, since he was there anyway, he read ten pages. Saturday, three things again, and twenty pages. It wasn't four chapters. But it was more than zero, and he wasn't in bed at noon.

qa.a: 'Revise four chapters a day'.

qa.a: Stuck and overwhelmed, lying in bed till noon, unable to face a plan that felt impossible.

qa.a: Talking to a counsellor or teacher about the heavy days, and slowly adding a small study goal while keeping the three basics.

qa.q: How might Hafsa feel getting Sumit's texts on Friday?
qa.a: Relieved and encouraged, seeing each small step done.

Warden's note, 3 March. Kishore, Block D.
This note is about two students in Room 214.
Since December, Divyansh has been going through a low patch. His roommate, Aman, became his only support: late-night talks most nights, walking him to class, answering texts during his own lectures. Divyansh told me he didn't want to 'bother' anyone else.
This week Aman came to me alone. He looked worn out. His own internals are next week, he hasn't slept properly in a month, and he has started staying in a friend's room to get some rest. 'I feel terrible, but I can't be everything,' he said.
Divyansh, meanwhile, feels abandoned and thinks Aman is angry with him.
I spoke to both separately today. Divyansh has agreed to see the counsellor this Thursday; I walked with him to book it, and he will call home this weekend. Aman is not to blame. I will meet both together next week.

qa.a: Abandoned, and worried that Aman is angry with him.

qa.a: Adding the counsellor, calls home and perhaps another friend, so no single person carries every low moment.

qa.q: What is it like for Aman?
qa.a: Aman is worn out and guilty, caring about Divyansh but unable to be everything, especially with his own exams coming.

passage:
Wednesday, 11 p.m. Vikas's diary.
Ganga moved her study table into the living room of our flat today. She said it's because of the light. I think it's because of me.
Since November she's been the one I call every time it gets dark in my head. 2 a.m., in the middle of her lab, the night before her interview. She always came. I never asked anyone else. My parents would worry, my college friends are busy, and Ganga just gets it.
Tonight I knocked and she said, 'Not tonight, Vikas, please.' She sounded so tired. I stood outside her door like an idiot.
I've been making her carry all of it. That's not fair to her, and it isn't even working for me, because now when she needs a break I've got nobody.
Tomorrow I'll go to the counselling centre and ask for an appointment. And I'll call Papa on Sunday, even if he worries.

qa.q: Where did Ganga move her study table?
qa.a: Into the living room of the flat.

qa.q: How did Vikas feel standing outside Ganga's door?
qa.a: Hurt and foolish at first, then guilty on realising how much Ganga had been carrying.

qa.q: Which other supports could Vikas add besides the counsellor and Papa?
qa.a: A college friend or a group activity, so there is more than one place to turn on dark days.

subtype: Approach: build a wider support net with roles [Revision]
passage:
When Neelam started leaving Yamini's messages on 'seen', Yamini knew. For three months her cousin had been her only lifeline through the low weeks at the teacher-training hostel in Sirsi: every tearful call, every sleepless night. Last Sunday Neelam finally said it: 'I love you, but I'm drained. I have my own exams.'
Yamini spent a day feeling ashamed. Then she took a sheet of paper and made a plan with more than one name on it.
The district hospital's counsellor, Wednesdays, booked through the hostel warden. A fixed call with Amma and Appa every Friday at eight, where she would actually tell them how she was. The women who walk around the temple tank at six every morning, whom the mess cook introduced her to.
With each one she said what she hoped for: listening on Wednesdays, just talking on Fridays, company in the mornings. And to Neelam she wrote: 'You're still my favourite person. Just not my only one.'

qa.q: When does the fixed call with Amma and Appa happen?
qa.a: Every Friday at eight.

qa.q: How did Yamini feel after Neelam said she was drained?
qa.a: Ashamed for a day, then determined to build a plan with more than one person in it.

qa.q: Why is telling each person what she hopes for a good step?
qa.a: It keeps each role clear and small, so no one is overwhelmed and Yamini knows whom to turn to for what.

qa.q: How might Neelam feel reading Yamini's message?
qa.a: Relieved and touched, freed from carrying everything while knowing she is still loved. 🤍

grounding: Shows a student, after a cousin's fatigue, adding a counsellor, a weekly family call and a walking group, and agreeing how each can help.
